Introduction
At the University of Giessen, inductively coupled ion sources were adapted as a thruster 
for spacecraft propulsion systems [1]. The radio-frequency ion thruster (RIT) gener­
ates the thrust by ejecting ions with a high velocity of up to 30 km/s. This type of ion 
thruster uses an inductive plasma discharge, which is the key to an extremely long life­
time. Featured with an extraction grid system for accelerating the ions, it enables a high 
specific impulse for good efficiency.
In past years, the RIT was miniaturized with a diameter in the range of a few centi­
metres leading to thrusts on the order of micro-Newtons (µN-RIT), which are needed 
for ultra-fine positioning of the spacecraft. In recent years, a Particle in cell (PIC) code 
named PlasmaPIC for the simulation of plasma in small-sized RF ion thruster has been 
developed [2]. PlasmaPIC employs massive parallelization to simulate multispecies

Abstract
A kinetic simulation of radio-frequency plasma is a highly sought-after tool for ion 
thrusters. A Particle-in-Cell code, named PlasmaPIC, has been developed to simulate 
plasma inside small-sized thrusters using massive parallelization running on a High-
Performance Computing Cluster. For particle-based simulation of the plasma in larger 
structures, the computational power increases rapidly. To overcome this limitation 
the variant named PlasmaPIC-Cyl is developed using polar coordinates that use either 
axisymmetry conditions or a partial 3D approach. In this paper, the 2.xD - approach 
which denotes the partial 3D domain, is described for the simulation of radio-
frequency ion thrusters. It has been used for the simulation of plasma properties 
like density, the temperature inside the plasma chamber and the extraction of the 
ion beam. The code is employed for the characterization of a radio frequency ion 
thruster, RIT-2.5, a thruster with a diameter of 2.5 cm. In this paper, the simulations are 
compared with the measurements to some extent to validate the numerical model. 
We further show its applicability in grid erosion calculations which can be used for 
the lifetime prediction of the gridded thrusters.
Keywords  Particle-in-Cell, Rf ion thruster, Cylindrical coordinates, Grid erosion

For the simulation of RIT-1.0, 100 × 100 × 100 grid points were used with 0.1 mm

To overcome this problem, the simulation domain is defined with reduced dimen­
sionality e.g. in 2D-PIC [5]. An RZ-symmetry is commonly used due to the cylindri­
cally symmetric nature of many thrusters [6, 7]. However, this is inefficient in the case 
of unsymmetric structures like spiralling coils or multi-aperture structures in the third 
dimension. We have developed a PIC code that uses a 3-dimensional cylindrical coor­
dinate system for modelling radio-frequency (RF) ion thrusters. The PlasmaPIC-Cyl 
takes advantage of the natural symmetry of the thruster and can be reduced into a 
partial domain (a Pie-section) in rotational θ direction or completely collapsed to RZ-
symmetry for faster calculations. The PlasmaPIC-Cyl is adapted in the cylindrical coor­
dinate system with an MPI-domain decomposition in the longitudinal z−direction. The 
Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) module is incorporated for neutral gas simula­
tion. Although the primary users would be the consortium of scientists working on RF 
ion thrusters at Justus Liebig University, the development of this code also targets the 
ion source or accelerator physics community and the scientists dealing with dense plas­
mas in cylinders for fusion research. In the following sections, we describe how the PIC 
in cylindrical coordinates, demonstrate RIT-2.5 simulation, and compare results from 
experiments. Finally, we present potential applications for grid erosion simulation.
Particle-in-Cell model in cylindrical polar coordinates
The PlasmaPIC-Cyl code is a Particle-in-Cell model in cylindrical polar coordinates. A 
single computational cycle of the PIC algorithm consists of particle mover, interpolation 
of charge and current source terms to the grid, computation of the fields on the grid 
points and finally interpolation of the fields from the grid to the particle locations [8].
The particles are initialized by assuming a homogeneous spatial distribution in 
the chamber volume and Maxwellian distribution of velocity. As the power is depos­
ited from an external RF coil, the phase-space distribution is evolved and the plasma is 
ignited along with a background neutral gas.

Cylindrical coordinate system
The spatial domain is defined using a standard cylindrical coordinate system. In the fol­
lowing sections we refer them as (r, θ, z)1.
As shown in the Fig. 1 the cylindrical domain is defined in such a way that the symme­
try axis coincides with the longitudinal axis of the thruster. Typically the spherical part 
of the thruster is aligned to the origin and the longitudinal distances are measured from 
the uppermost point.

As shown in Fig. 3, a first order charge distribution is implemented using volume-
weighting. For regular cells, the volume element is given as dV = r dr dθ dz which 
depends upon the radial position of the cell. The volume of the axis cell is simply 
dV = π dr2 dz /Nθ, where Nθ is the number of grid points in the azimuthal direction. 
To interpolate field quantities from grid points to particle positions in continuous coor­
dinates, the linear weighting scheme is used backwards for a self-consistent algorithm. 
In case of vector fields it has to incorporate the change of basis vectors, while transform­
ing vector field components from grid points to continuous coordinates. For the com­
putation of the dynamic electromagnetic fields, individual vector field components are 
defined on a staggered grid (Yee-grid) [9].

Particle mover
The PlasmaPIC-Cyl uses the Boris method to move particles [11]. It is an explicit 
method, employing a leap-frog algorithm, with a high long-term accuracy. Compared to 
an implicit method it requires less computational resources and is suited for simulation 
comprising a large particle number.
For particle motion in a cylindrical coordinate system, the Boris method must be 
adapted to account for the change in basis vectors in curvilinear coordinates. This can 
be done by introducing an intermediate step, where the new position coordinates are 
computed, before the velocity vector components can be expressed in terms of new basis 
vectors. A brief discussion of the relevant equations for the Boris mover in Cartesian 
and cylindrical geometries can be found in Appendix A. For a more detailed analysis of 
the Boris mover in a cylindrical geometry, please refer to [12].

For electron-neutral interactions, three collision types are taken into account. These

The resulting energy and the momentum redistribution of species has been imple­

For the modelling of the neutral gas distribution with reduced particle-particle inter­
actions, the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method is well suited [16]. The

It can also be applied for molecular flow without losing accuracy but it is computation­

As in a PIC algorithm, the particles are represented by super-particles and space-time 
domains are discretized. The velocity of a particle in DSMC is changed in particle-par­
ticle or particle-wall collisions only. The No Time Counter method is used for a reduced 
number of operations [18].
In this presented work, the neutral gas distribution is simulated till a stable flow is 
achieved. Then using the neutral gas density, electron-neutral and ion-neutral interac­
tions are calculated in each cell.
Geometry representation
In the current format, the object geometries are defined manually. The nodes on the 
cylindrical mesh are declared as either material or a particular region of interest corre­
sponding to their location in the cylindrical domain. Thus instead of a sugar cube model 
as in cartesian coordinates, we construct a model with concentric cylindrical elements. 
PlasmaPIC-Cyl currently supports four object definitions with properties as follows:
 	•
Equipotential: In this case, the node points are defined with fixed potentials e.g. 
thruster’s wall, extraction grid etc. The charged particles are removed if they strike 
such objects. This treatment corresponds to an ideal voltage source. The neutral 
atoms are just bounced back with an appropriate deflected velocity component.
 	•
Dielectric: A dielectric object is an insulator. For every dielectric surface, a specific 
permittivity is considered which can be user-defined.
 	•
Plasma region: All the nodes inside the plasma chamber correspond to this category 
where charge densities, potential and consequently fields are to be calculated in every 
time step.
 	•
Beam region: Typically all the nodes outside the plasma region, excluding material 
nodes, can be considered as a beam region. In this region, the extracted ion beams or 
the exhaust plume can be simulated.
In the Cartesian version of this code (PlasmaPIC), a particular node location is deter­
mined within the CAD object and attributed appropriate geometric entity. This is done 
by reading tetrahedral elements and surfaces generated using graphics software (Free­
CAD). The updated version of the PlasmaPIC-Cyl will also include a similar subrou­
tine so that a CAD file can be imported to determine the node types in the cylindrical 
domain. Figure 4 shows the CAD model of RIT-2.5 and its equivalent representation in

Domain decomposition and n-fold symmetry
For parallel processing, the domain is decomposed in a longitudinal z-direction using a 
Message Parsing Interface (MPI). Thus each processor has its number of particles within 
the specified simulation domain. While the parallelization by domain decomposition 
generally leads to a drastic decrease in the computation time of field solvers and particle 
mover, this speed-up wears out for large numbers of processes. Depending on the num­
ber of grid points in the z-direction and the z-range of the domain, there is a saturation 
limit for the speed-up in terms of number of processes. For field solvers, the number of 
processes should not exceed the grid point number. For the particle mover, the z-range 
of a process should not drop below a certain limit, otherwise the particle exchange takes 
longer than the particle movement.
As the extraction grids feature a six-fold symmetry, it allows us to omit 5/6 of the 
θ-range in the simulation domain, without considerable loss of information associated 
with the extraction process. However, since the rf-frequency coils are not axisymmetric 
in a real RIT-2.5, a complete coil is implemented even when a partial domain is simu­
lated. Simulation of restricted range θ ∈[0, π/3) is advantageous for a speed-up, and 
cuts the simulation time to about 1/6 of the full range execution time. The periodicity in 
θ direction can be achieved by treating θ = 0 equally to θ = π/3 instead of θ = 2π in the 
case of a restricted θ-range.
Numerical modelling of RIT-2.5 thruster
Here we have characterized, the RIT-2.5 thruster, the number representing the diam­
eter of 2.5 cm of the thruster. The discharge chamber consists of a dome shape on one 
side and a cylinder at the extraction side. The dome is a half-sphere with a radius of 
12.5 mm. The radius of the cylindrical part is the same as the radius of the spherical 
part. The cylindrical part of the discharge chamber is 9.9 mm long. The induction coil, 
coupling the rf-power into the plasma, consists of 8 individual coils surrounding the 
plasma chamber, out of which 4 coils are placed around the cylindrical part and 4 coils 
around the dome part of the plasma chamber. The extraction section consists of two 
grids spaced 0.85 mm apart, with a thickness of 0.25 mm and 1.5 mm, respectively. 
Each has 37 extraction holes, arranged in six-fold symmetry, with radii 0.95 mm (first 
grid) and 0.6 mm (second grid).
RIT-2.5 has a gas inlet on the periphery of near extraction. For the simulation, we 
define a domain with a radius of 16.0 mm and a length of 35.0 mm. At a distance of 
7.25 mm from the second grid of the extraction assembly, we define a detector which 
counts particles reaching every time step. In the case of ion extraction, it can be regarded 
as a Faraday cup for the current measurement.
DSMC simulation of RIT-2.5 thruster
For background gas distribution, the DSMC module was initiated prior. Neutral Xenon 
particles (Xe0) with a mass flow of 6.54 × 10−10 kg/s are injected inside the plasma 
chamber through an inlet located at the periphery of the chamber wall near extrac­
tion grid with a temperature of 300 K. Neutral gas simulations were performed using

tions allow us to define a larger step for neutral particles. The module execution was 
stopped when a constant particle flow at the detector was achieved after 1 ms, which

The cylindrical domain consists of 51 × 2 × 251 mesh points in r, θ and longitudinal 
z-direction, respectively. This corresponds to the step size 3.20 × 10−04 m in the radial 
direction and 1.40 × 10−04 m in the longitudinal direction. About 240 processors were 
used for parallel computation over a time of 16,639 seconds.

Plasma simulation of RIT-2.5 thruster
For the plasma simulation inside an ion thruster, the ions and electrons are spatially pop­
ulated inside the chamber homogeneously and the velocities follow Maxwell’s distribu­
tion. For collisions with neutrals, the pre-calculated phase-space distribution of neutrals 
is assumed, as discussed in the earlier section. Although the neutral gas density can fluc­
tuate during plasma ignition, this paper presumes, it remains constant. Consequently, 
the DSMC module is implemented solely at the start, ensuring a clear focus on the ini­
tial conditions for more accurate analysis. The external power is deposited through the 
induction coil. The simulations run typically in the range of a few µs to build a stable 
plasma. The initial parameters are chosen, which could be used for experiments with 
RIT-2.5 for characterization and the numerical model can be compared.

Comparison with measurements
The experiments were arranged to measure temperature, density and extraction currents 
from RIT2.52. The experiments generated a large set of data for different values of input 
mass flow, RF power and extraction voltages. Out of which we selected the data corre­
sponding to the plasma density of 1 × 1015/m3.
The simulations were performed using this density and restricting the domain to 30∘ 
sector. The extracted currents range from 3.5 mA to 5.4 mA when the power is varied 
between22.0 W and 46.6 W. This is achieved with an extraction voltage of 1200 V and 
a mass flow of 0.16 sccm. Additionally, with a neutral gas (Xe0) flow rate of 0.16 sccm 
and a power setting of 30 W, the extracted current varies between 4.7 mA and 4.9 mA 
as the extraction voltage increases from 1000 V to 1500 V. Since the simulated currents 
will match with experiments as our domain is restricted, we compared the normalized 
extracted current instead of absolute values.
Figure 10 a) shows the increasing extraction current as a function of the extraction 
voltage. The neutral gas (Xe0) flow of 0.24 sccm was injected and 22 W power coupled 
to ignite the plasma. For this case plasma temperature of 4 eV  was measured and with 
the same value simulated. Figure 10 b) shows the increasing extraction current as a func­
tion of the plasma temperature and a consequent fall in the curve. Although the mea­
sured curve does not follow exact curve, it does show rise and then the fall.

PlasmaPIC-Cyl for grid erosion calculations
Although the PlasmaPIC-Cyl is developed for plasma simulation in any larger struc­
tures, it can be very efficiently used for erosion studies and life-expectancy calculation 
for gridded ion thrusters. The lifetime of the gridded ion thruster is a pivotal issue and 
the numerical model can vastly reduce experimental efforts [19]. The grid erosion is 
caused due to the bombardment of the strayed ions [20]. Charge exchange (CEX) may 
occur between extracted fast ions and slow neutral particles in the extraction region. 
The ions with newly acquired charge have lower momentum and are attracted to the 
negative potential of the acceleration grid. These ions impact the grid surface with ener­
gies above the sputtering threshold of the material causing erosion and ultimately deg­
radation. Although erosion implies the sputtering and degradation of the grid material 
depending upon energy flux here we are demonstrating the particle bombardment and 
distribution only.
For erosion calculation, Xenon plasma with different densities was simulated through­
out about 9 µs and the number of particles, namely the ions, hitting the grid was 
counted. Figure 11 a) shows the particle distribution hitting the grid of the 30∘ sector. 
The dark green dotted line shows the position of grid apertures. The graph depicts the 
mesh edges, one can extract valuable information by counting the number of particles 
along the radial axis. Figure 11 b) shows the ion distribution along the radial axis at 
θ = 4◦.
It validates that the maximum erosion occurs at the radially inner edge of the periph­
eral extraction aperture. It also indicates the extent of the erosion depends upon the 
plasma density.
Figure 12 shows the number of particles striking the grid as a function of plasma den­
sity for two different cases. In Fig. 12 a) the number of particles hitting the outer edge

Conclusion
In this paper, we have described our particle-based PlasmaPIC-Cyl code for kinetic 
modelling of the plasmas. It is used to study the xenon plasma inside an RIT-2.5 ion 
thruster and the extracted ion beams. The code is versatile and can be used for many 
applications in plasma physics which demand for high performance computing. The 
variable θ-domain approach helps faster calculation of larger structures with cylindri­
cal symmetry. From the comparison with the measurements, one can conclude that we 
have a reliable tool for further research. We have demonstrated that it can used for grid 
erosion simulation which is a power feature for the prediction of a gridded ion thruster 
lifetime.

Abstract: A kinetic simulation of radio-frequency plasma is a highly sought-after tool for ion thrusters. A Particle-in-Cell code, named PlasmaPIC, has been developed to simulate plasma inside small-sized thrusters using massive parallelization running on a High- Performance Computing Cluster. For particle-based simulation of the plasma in larger structures, the computational power increases rapidly. To overcome this limitation the variant named PlasmaPIC-Cyl is developed using polar coordinates that use either axisymmetry conditions or a partial 3D approach. In this paper, the 2.xD - approach which denotes the partial 3D domain, is described for the simulation of radio- frequency ion thrusters. It has been used for the simulation of plasma properties like density, the temperature inside the plasma chamber and the extraction of the ion beam. The code is employed for the characterization of a radio frequency ion thruster, RIT-2.5, a thruster with a diameter of 2.5 cm. In this paper, the simulations are compared with the measurements to some extent to validate the numerical model. We further show its applicability in grid erosion calculations which can be used for the lifetime prediction of the gridded thrusters.
